2024 · TMLR · Benchmarks & Evals

Long-context LLMs Struggle with Long In-context Learning

Fifteen long-context LLMs — 7B open-source models built with every context-extension trick in circulation, plus GPT4-turbo, GPT4o, Claude3-Opus, and Gemini-1.5-Pro's 10-million-token window — are put through in-context classification over label spaces of 28 to 174 classes instead of passkey retrieval or document QA. On the hardest of the six tasks, Discovery (174 discourse-marker classes), every open-source model and three of the four frontier API models score at or near zero; the best result anywhere is Gemini-1.5-Pro's 14.0% accuracy, against 87.4% for a fully fine-tuned classifier on the same labels.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Long-context LLMs are marketed on the size of their context windows — Gemini-1.5-Pro's is advertised at up to 10 million tokens — but the paper argues the standard ways of testing that capacity are all gameable. Three evaluation families dominate the literature: language-model perplexity over long documents; synthetic retrieval tasks like passkey retrieval and needle-in-a-haystack, where several models already clear 99%+; and long-document question-answering or summarization over corpora like Qasper. None of the three actually forces a model to hold the entire input in working memory. Perplexity is a poor proxy for downstream task ability. Passkey retrieval only requires locating one inserted string. And in long-document QA, a model can take a shortcut straight to the short passage containing the answer without reading the rest of the document, while summarization models lean on a similar lead-sentence position bias (Nallapati et al., 2017) instead of genuine long-range comprehension — the same general shortcut-ability the paper's own exploratory experiment revisits via the "lost in the middle" phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023).

The authors' fix is to repurpose in-context learning (ICL) on extreme-label classification. Give a model K examples per label, drawn from a fine-grained label space that can run into the hundreds of classes, and ask it to classify a held-out instance. Because every label needs its own demonstrations to disambiguate, and because a correct prediction requires the model to have recognized the entire label space rather than just the instance closest to the query, extreme-label ICL cannot be solved by reading a short snippet — it requires scanning and integrating the whole demonstration set. That is the concrete gap LongICLBench targets: a benchmark where a correct answer is itself evidence of whole-context comprehension, not local retrieval.

// how it works

The method

LongICLBench assembles six existing classification datasets spanning 28 to 174 classes: GoEmotions (28 emotion labels), BANKING77 (77 banking intents), TacRED (41 relation types), Few-NERD (66 fine-grained entity types), DialogRE (36 dialogue relation types), and Discovery (174 discourse-marker types). Demonstration sets are built in "rounds": one round (1R) is a complete pass through every distinct label with exactly one example each, and each additional round adds one more example per label, so 5R gives five demonstrations per label. Because a higher-cardinality label space needs more tokens just to be traversed once, stepping through rounds on the same dataset produces a controlled ladder of context lengths — from roughly 2K tokens (BANKING77, 1R) up to 50K tokens (Discovery, 5R) across the four datasets that get main-body result tables. Test sets are 500 examples per dataset, sampled to keep the label distribution even, and every model is evaluated against the exact same demonstration and test sets so the comparison is apples-to-apples.

Fifteen long-context LLMs are evaluated: eleven ~7B open-source models covering nearly every context-extension strategy in circulation — position interpolation (LLaMA-2-7B-32K), NTK-aware interpolation (Qwen-1.5-7B-base), shifted short attention (LLaMA-2-7B-LongLora), dynamic NTK (InternLM2-7B-base), the Focused Transformer approach (Long-LLaMA-code-7B), plus the two non-Transformer architectures RWKV-5-World and Mamba-2.8B — and four frontier API models, GPT4-turbo and GPT4o (128K support), Claude3-Opus (200K), and Gemini-1.5-Pro (10M). Scoring uses Accuracy for GoEmotion, BANKING77, and Discovery, and F1 for the two relation-extraction datasets (TacRED, DialogRE) and the entity-recognition dataset (Few-NERD).

Beyond the headline accuracy/F1 numbers, the paper runs an exploratory position analysis on TacRED at 3 rounds (123 demonstrations total: 41 labels × 3). First, demonstrations of the same label are scattered randomly through the prompt and each label's resulting test accuracy is tracked against where its examples happened to fall; then the same demonstrations are re-ordered so that same-label instances sit adjacent to each other ("grouped"), and the resulting accuracy shift is measured per model. The aim is to separate a model's sensitivity to where in the prompt a label's evidence sits from its sensitivity to how it's distributed.

// what they found

The results

The headline pattern is a difficulty ladder across the four datasets that get main-body tables (Figure 1, Figure 3). On the easiest, BANKING77 (2K–14K tokens, Accuracy), a minority of models improve substantially as rounds increase — 6 of the 15 gain end-to-end from 1R to 5R, and roughly 8 of 15 peak above their 1R score by a real margin — with LLaMA-2-7B-32K rising from 30.2% (1R) to 77.2% (5R) and Gemini-1.5-Pro climbing from 28.8% (1R) to a peak of 82.2% (3R). But two models fail outright at every round on every one of the four main tables: LLaMA-2-7B-LongLora and Mamba-2.8B both score exactly 0 throughout. A third, Gemma-7B-base, is 0 on BANKING77 and Discovery but not everywhere — it manages 14.7 F1 on DialogRE's shortest round and 0.4 F1 on TacRED's first two rounds before falling to 0.

On TacRED (4K–18K tokens, F1) and DialogRE (8K–32K tokens, F1) — both requiring the model to track argument pairs across a whole relation-extraction label set rather than a single intent — every open-source model trails GPT4-turbo, GPT4o, and Gemini-1.5-Pro at nearly every round — sometimes by a wide margin, sometimes narrowly (DialogRE 1R: Mistral-7B-v0.2-base's 24.0 F1 vs. Gemini-1.5-Pro's 29.6, a 5.6-point gap) — though not Claude3-Opus: its own decline is steep enough that Mistral-7B-v0.2-base, a 7B open model, outscores it at 2 of 5 rounds on TacRED (51.6 vs. 35.4 at 3R; 48.0 vs. 43.4 at 4R) and 4 of 5 rounds on DialogRE (24.0 vs. 16.8 at 1R; 23.2 vs. 15.3 at 3R; 22.0 vs. 0.8 at 4R; 21.1 vs. 0 at 5R). The paper itself notes that "only GPT4-turbo and GPT4o can consistently benefit from more demonstrations" while the rest peak around the middle of the round range (context length 13K–25K) and then decline. GPT4-turbo's own trajectory does climb monotonically in both tables (TacRED: 74.4 → 76.5 → 79.5 → 80.4 → 84.2 F1; DialogRE: 42.9 → 47.8 → 52.0 → 55.9 → 57.7 F1). Gemini-1.5-Pro and Claude3-Opus, by contrast, are not monotonic in either table — Gemini's TacRED F1 rises to 81.4 (2R), dips to 79.6 (3R), then climbs again to 82.3 by 5R, and Claude3-Opus's DialogRE F1 rises to 30.3 (2R) before collapsing to 0 (5R).

On the hardest dataset, Discovery (174 discourse-marker classes, 10K–50K tokens, Accuracy), every model collapses. All eleven open-source models score 0 or effectively 0 at every round. Among the four API models, only Gemini-1.5-Pro reaches double digits, and only at the shortest length: 14.0% at 1R (10K tokens), falling to 6.0%, 3.2%, 1.8%, and 2.8% as context grows to 5R (50K tokens) — its own best score on Discovery is its very first data point, and more demonstrations make it worse rather than better. GPT4-turbo, GPT4o, and Claude3-Opus never exceed 2.8% on Discovery at any round. A fully fine-tuned baseline — Table 6 lists it as SoTA ("MTL," 87.4%), and the paper's introduction separately describes "a fine-tuned BERT model (Kenton & Toutanova, 2019)" reaching the same ~87% on this task — beats every few-shot LLM by a wide margin, roughly six times Gemini-1.5-Pro's best few-shot number.

Discovery (174 classes, Accuracy %) — the four frontier API models across all five rounds, plus the fully-supervised baseline. The exploratory position analysis adds a second axis: it isn't only length that hurts, but how same-label demonstrations are arranged. Reorganizing TacRED's 3-round demonstrations (123 instances, still ~10K tokens) so that same-label instances sit adjacent instead of scattered randomly through the prompt drops F1 for most models — most severely for Mistral-7B-v0.2-base, from 51.6 (scattered) down to 5.1 (grouped), a 46.5-point fall and the largest drop anywhere in that experiment. GPT4-turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro are not immune either, losing 20.3 and 22.3 points respectively. A minority of models — LLaMA-2-7B-32K and RWKV-5-World — actually gain a couple of points (+2.6 each) under grouping.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

LongICLBench earns its place because it resists exactly the shortcuts that undermine passkey retrieval and lost-in-the-middle-style QA: getting a single Discovery prediction right requires having processed enough of the 174-label space to recognize it, not just found one relevant sentence. The Discovery result — Gemini-1.5-Pro's 14.0% against a fully fine-tuned classifier's 87.4% — is a clean, legible number precisely because it can't be explained away by a retrieval shortcut. But a few places in the paper's own framing don't survive a check against its own tables, and a few real gaps are left entirely unaddressed.

Start with the paper's own consistency: "only GPT4-turbo and GPT4o can consistently benefit from more demonstrations" is the claim made about Tables 4 and 5 (TacRED and DialogRE). GPT4-turbo's trajectory really is monotonically increasing in both (74.4→76.5→79.5→80.4→84.2 F1 on TacRED; 42.9→47.8→52.0→55.9→57.7 F1 on DialogRE) — but GPT4o's is not, in either table. On TacRED, GPT4o goes 71.1 → 75.5 → 73.6 → 73.2 → 72.3 F1: it peaks at 2R and declines for three straight rounds. On DialogRE it goes 40.6 → 41.5 → 41.0 → 47.3 → 45.3 F1: a dip at 3R, a rise, then a fall. Of the two models singled out for "consistent" benefit from more context, only one of them actually is consistent by the paper's own numbers.

More substantively, the benchmark's core manipulation — adding "rounds" — changes two things at once: it increases both the number of demonstrations per label (more contrastive signal for ICL) and the raw token count (more context to process). The paper never separates these. A model that degrades from 1R to 5R on Discovery could be suffering from long-context degradation, from ICL saturation/dilution as the demonstration set grows regardless of length, or from both — and nothing in the design distinguishes them. A controlled variant that held token count fixed while varying label coverage (or vice versa) would make the "long context" attribution much sharper.

Contamination is not discussed anywhere in the paper. All six component datasets — GoEmotions, BANKING77, TacRED, Few-NERD, DialogRE, Discovery — are public releases dating from 2017 (TacRED) to 2021 (Few-NERD), and are near-certain to appear somewhere in the pretraining corpora of every evaluated model, whether as raw text, as a labeled dataset card, or via papers-with-code-style summaries. That cuts both ways: the near-uniform collapse on Discovery is at least not an obvious case of memorized-label cheating, but the paper offers no canary or perturbation check to actually verify that, and a reader is left inferring it from the results rather than being shown it.

baselines

The 15 few-shot LLMs are compared fairly against each other on identical demonstration/test sets. But the "SoTA" rows quoted per dataset (BERT 58.9 on GoEmotion, RoBERTa+ICDA 94.4 on BANKING77, DeepStruct 76.8 on TacRED, HiDialog 77.1 on DialogRE, MTL 87.4 on Discovery, PL-Marker 70.9 on Few-NERD) are single numbers with no stated training-set size, so a reader can't calibrate how many labeled examples full fine-tuning needed — and on five of the six datasets it did beat every few-shot LLM; on TacRED it didn't, since GPT4-turbo's own best few-shot F1 (84.2 at 5R) exceeds the quoted DeepStruct SoTA (76.8).

contamination

Not addressed. All six datasets are public releases dating from 2017 to 2021, plausibly present somewhere in every evaluated model's pretraining data; no canary, perturbation, or leakage check is reported.

what's missed

"Rounds" conflate label-count and token-count in one knob, so the paper can't cleanly attribute performance decay to context length specifically. No prompt-robustness check across the six bespoke templates (Table 9), no demonstration-resampling variance on a 500-example test set, and no finer error analysis of why Discovery collapses (label confusion vs. refusal vs. hitting an undocumented practical context limit below the advertised window).

would raise confidence

An ablation that separates token count from class count; a contamination/canary check given all six datasets predate every model's training cutoff; multiple demonstration draws per round to bound variance; and resolving the GPT4o monotonicity claim against its own printed numbers.

// bottom line

LongICLBench's central idea — that extreme-label ICL forces whole-context comprehension in a way retrieval and QA-style long-context evals don't — is a genuine methodological contribution, and the Discovery result is a striking, hard-to-dismiss number. The paper's writing occasionally overclaims uniformity where the tables show more texture (the GPT4o "consistency" claim being the clearest case), and it leaves the length-vs-label-count confound and contamination risk unexamined, but neither undermines the core finding: at 50K tokens and 174 classes, none of the fifteen evaluated LLMs come close to what a fine-tuned classifier gets on the same data.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. Extreme-label in-context classification is a context-length stress test that resists the shortcuts — short-snippet retrieval, lead-sentence bias — that undermine QA- and summarization-based long-context evaluations, because getting any single prediction right requires having scanned the entire label space first.
  2. The gap is starkest on the hardest task: Gemini-1.5-Pro tops the field on Discovery (174 discourse-marker classes) at just 14.0% accuracy, with every other evaluated LLM at or near 0%, against 87.4% for a fully fine-tuned classifier on the identical labels — the widest few-shot-vs-fine-tuned gap the paper reports.
  3. Performance depends on how demonstrations are arranged, not just how many there are: grouping same-label instances together (instead of scattering them through the prompt) costs GPT4-turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro 20+ F1 points on TacRED, and costs Mistral-7B-v0.2-base 46.5 points — a genuine position/recency sensitivity distinct from raw context-length capacity.
